To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the products of benzo(a)pyrene-DNA binding in mouse embryo cells are not the same as the products of reaction of benzo(a)-pyrene-4.5-oxide with mouse embryo DNA, and that the products of binding of benzo(a]pyrene to mouse embryo DNA are not the same in mouse embryo cells and mouse embryo DNA in aqueous solution.

the hydrocarbon-deoxynucleoside products of the reaction of DNA with benzo(alpha)-pyrene-4.5-oxide are different from the hydrocarbon-deoxygenucleoside products formed in DNA that is isolated from mouse embryo cells treated with benzo(alpha-)pyrene.
the products of the metabolic activation of [3H]BP to DNA bound products are not the same as the products formed by direct addition of BP 4,5-epoxide to DNA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the metabolism of benzo(alpha)-pyrene by cultured mouse embryo cells and with the products formed when this hydrocarbon becomes covalently bound with DNA.
the identification and quantitation of hydrocarbon-deoxyribose adducts formed by the metabolic activation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and their subsequent binding to cellular DNA.

the identification of DNA-bound benzo(alpha) pyrene products formed in mouse embryo cells treated with [3 H]benzo(alpha)-pyrene, and with a comparison of those products with the products formed when benzo(alpha) -pyrene-4.5-oxide is reacted with DNA in vitro in an aqueous ethanol solution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DNA-bound products formed from benzo(alpha) pyrene in mouse embryo cells were not the same as those formed by the reaction between benzo(alpha) -pyrene-4.5-oxide and DNA.
the DNA-bound products formed by reaction of benzo(a)pyrene and benzo(a) pyrene-4, 5-oxide with the DNA of mouse embryo cells in vitro are not the same.

the DNA of mouse embryo cells treated in culture with benzo(alpha)-pyrene is modified by the formation of hydrocarbons covalently linked to the deoxyribonucieotide residues, and that these hydrocarbons are not formed by the reaction with DNA of benzo(alpha)- pyrene-4, 5-oxide.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
benzo(alpha) pyrene does not form covalent bonds with DNA in mouse embryo cell cultures, whereas benzo(alpha) p yrene-4, 5-oxide does.

benzo(alpha) pyrene is activated in cultured mouse embryo cells to a reactive intermediate which binds covalently to DNA and that the major DNA-bound product is the same in both mouse embryo cells in tissue culture and in mouse skin.

the metabolic activation in the cells of benzo(alpha)-pyrene to a form that reacts covalently with cellular DNA involves a process that is more complex than simply the formation of the K-region epoxide.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the metabolic activation pathway of benzo(alpha)-pyrene in mouse embryo cells is different from that which results in the formation of the K-region epoxide, which is the presumed reactive metabolite in the reaction of benz(alpha)pyrene and DNA in the aqueous ethanol system.
we have developed a method to study the metabolic activation of a carcinogen by using the DNA that has been covalently bound by the carcinogen in a living system.
